0:0.caption: Our fitness app needs a separate profile for each person.
0:0.spoken: Our fitness app needs a separate profile for each person.

0:1.caption: Each profile keeps a name, a height and a weight together, and can calculate a BMI from its own values.
0:1.spoken: Each profile keeps a name, a height and a weight together, and can calculate a B M I from its own values.

0:2.caption: Week three: creating a fitness profile with a class.
0:2.spoken: Week three: creating a fitness profile with a class.

1:0.caption: Chapter one: start with a familiar function.
1:0.spoken: Chapter one: start with a familiar function.

1:1.caption: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres, squared. Squared means height times itself.
1:1.spoken: B M I is weight in kilograms divided by height in meters, squared. Squared means height times itself.

1:2.caption: Picture it as a square: 1.75 metres on each side gives an area of 3.0625 square metres.
1:2.spoken: Picture it as a square: one point seven five meters on each side gives an area of three point zero six two five square meters.

1:3.caption: Share 70 kilograms over that area: 22.86. That's Sam's BMI.
1:3.spoken: Share 70 kilograms over that area: twenty two point eight six. That's Sam's B M I.

1:4.caption: But the app has to keep every person's measurements. As loose variables, which height belongs to whom?
1:4.spoken: But the app has to keep every person's measurements. As loose variables, which height belongs to whom?

1:5.caption: What we want is to keep each person's values together, in one profile.
1:5.spoken: What we want is to keep each person's values together, in one profile.

2:0.caption: Chapter two: a class and its objects.
2:0.spoken: Chapter two: a class and its objects.

2:1.caption: A class defines a kind of object. FitnessProfile is the template: which values a profile holds, and what it can do.
2:1.spoken: A class defines a kind of object. FitnessProfile is the template: which values a profile holds, and what it can do.

2:2.caption: An object, also called an instance, is one particular example made from that class. This one is Sam's profile.
2:2.spoken: An object, also called an instance, is one particular example made from that class. This one is Sam's profile.

2:3.caption: An attribute is a value stored on an object, like Sam's height.
2:3.spoken: An attribute is a value stored on an object, like Sam's height.

2:4.caption: A method is a function defined inside the class. calculate_bmi works with this profile's own values.
2:4.spoken: A method is a function defined inside the class. calculate underscore B M I works with this profile's own values.

2:5.caption: One class, as many objects as we need, each holding its own values.
2:5.spoken: One class, as many objects as we need, each holding its own values.

3:0.caption: Chapter three: reading the class, one part at a time.
3:0.spoken: Chapter three: reading the class, one part at a time.

3:1.caption: class FitnessProfile names the class. Capital letters set class names apart from variable names.
3:1.spoken: class FitnessProfile names the class. Capital letters set class names apart from variable names.

3:2.caption: __init__, with two underscores on each side, is the initialisation method. Python calls it whenever we create a profile.
3:2.spoken: dunder init, with two underscores on each side, is the initialisation method. Python calls it whenever we create a profile.

3:3.caption: self refers to the particular object being set up or used. self.height_m means the height stored on this profile.
3:3.spoken: self refers to the particular object being set up or used. self dot height underscore meters means the height stored on this profile.

3:4.caption: self.name = name stores the value we pass in as an attribute on the new object. Same for height and weight.
3:4.spoken: self dot name equals name stores the value we pass in as an attribute on the new object. Same for height and weight.

3:5.caption: calculate_bmi is a method, because it sits inside the class. It reads this object's attributes and returns a result.
3:5.spoken: calculate underscore B M I is a method, because it sits inside the class. It reads this object's attributes and returns a result.

3:6.caption: Watch the two indentation levels: methods sit four spaces in, and their instructions another four.
3:6.spoken: Watch the two indentation levels: methods sit four spaces in, and their instructions another four.

4:1.caption: Calling the class name creates an object. A fresh profile is stamped out from the template.
4:1.spoken: Calling the class name creates an object. A fresh profile is stamped out from the template.

4:2.caption: Python runs __init__ and supplies self automatically: self is this brand-new profile.
4:2.spoken: Python runs dunder init and supplies self automatically: self is this brand-new profile.

4:3.caption: Our three arguments line up with the parameters after self: name, height, weight.
4:3.spoken: Our three arguments line up with the parameters after self: name, height, weight.

4:4.caption: self.name = name stores Sam on this profile. Then the height, 1.75, and the weight, 70.0.
4:4.spoken: self dot name equals name stores Sam on this profile. Then the height, one point seven five, and the weight, seventy point zero.

4:5.caption: The variable sam_profile now refers to one complete object.
4:5.spoken: The variable sam underscore profile now refers to one complete object.

5:0.caption: Chapter five: dot notation and methods.
5:0.spoken: Chapter five: dot notation and methods.

5:1.caption: A dot connects an object to one of its attributes. sam_profile.name follows the tag to this profile and reads the name stored there.
5:1.spoken: A dot connects an object to one of its attributes. sam underscore profile dot name follows the tag to this profile and reads the name stored there.

5:2.caption: sam_profile.height_m reads the height: 1.75 metres.
5:2.spoken: sam underscore profile dot height underscore meters reads the height: one point seven five meters.

5:3.caption: Add parentheses and the dot calls a method instead. calculate_bmi runs with self set to Sam's profile…
5:3.spoken: Add parentheses and the dot calls a method instead. calculate underscore B M I runs with self set to Sam's profile...

5:4.caption: …so self.weight_kg and self.height_m are Sam's own stored values. 70 divided by 1.75 squared: 22.86.
5:4.spoken: ...so self dot weight underscore kilograms and self dot height underscore meters are Sam's own stored values. 70 divided by one point seven five squared: twenty two point eight six.

5:5.caption: Notice the call needs no measurement arguments. They're already stored in the object.
5:5.spoken: Notice the call needs no measurement arguments. They're already stored in the object.

6:0.caption: Chapter six: a second profile, and an update.
6:0.spoken: Chapter six: a second profile, and an update.

6:1.caption: Same class, second object. Alex's profile follows the same definition but stores its own values.
6:1.spoken: Same class, second object. Alex's profile follows the same definition but stores its own values.

6:2.caption: The same method on Alex's object uses Alex's measurements: 25.0.
6:2.spoken: The same method on Alex's object uses Alex's measurements: twenty five point zero.

6:3.caption: Update one profile by assigning to its attribute. Sam's weight becomes 72.0.
6:3.spoken: Update one profile by assigning to its attribute. Sam's weight becomes seventy two point zero.

6:4.caption: And Alex's weight? Still 64.0. Each object keeps its own values.
6:4.spoken: And Alex's weight? Still sixty four point zero. Each object keeps its own values.

6:5.caption: The method reads the stored values every time it runs, so recalculating gives 23.51.
6:5.spoken: The method reads the stored values every time it runs, so recalculating gives twenty three point five one.

6:6.caption: But sam_bmi, calculated earlier, still holds 22.86. The new result lives in updated_sam_bmi.
6:6.spoken: But sam underscore B M I, calculated earlier, still holds twenty two point eight six. The new result lives in updated underscore sam underscore B M I.

7:0.caption: Chapter seven: a profile summary, and a common error.
7:0.spoken: Chapter seven: a profile summary, and a common error.

7:1.caption: Read the attributes, call the method, and we have a small profile card as text.
7:1.spoken: Read the attributes, call the method, and we have a small profile card as text.

7:2.caption: Change sam_profile to alex_profile on every line, and the same code summarises Alex instead. Note that 1.60 prints as 1.6.
7:2.spoken: Change sam underscore profile to alex underscore profile on every line, and the same code summarises Alex instead. Note that one point six zero prints as one point six.

7:3.caption: Watch out: the name after the dot must exist on the object. sam_profile.weight looks for a weight slot, but there's only weight_kg.
7:3.spoken: Watch out: the name after the dot must exist on the object. sam underscore profile dot weight looks for a weight slot, but there's only weight underscore kilograms.

7:4.caption: That's an AttributeError. Check the spelling against the class definition. Python even suggests the right name.
7:4.spoken: That's an attribute error. Check the spelling against the class definition. Python even suggests the right name.

8:0.caption: Let's recap, and then it's your turn.
8:0.spoken: Let's recap, and then it's your turn.

8:1.caption: A class groups related data and behaviour. Each profile object has its own attributes. And a method uses self to work with the object it was called on.
8:1.spoken: A class groups related data and behaviour. Each profile object has its own attributes. And a method uses self to work with the object it was called on.

8:2.caption: Exercise one: add two profiles. Create Jordan, 1.80 metres and 81 kilos, and Casey, 1.60 and 64. Call each one's BMI method.
8:2.spoken: Exercise one: add two profiles. Create Jordan, one point eight zero meters and 81 kilos, and Casey, one point six zero and 64. Call each one's B M I method.

8:3.caption: Exercise two: correct a measurement. Taylor's weight was entered as 80. Update it to 81, then calculate the BMI again.
8:3.spoken: Exercise two: correct a measurement. Taylor's weight was entered as 80. Update it to 81, then calculate the B M I again.
